# pathland-view (Java) — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 27, 2026

The hand-written, framework-agnostic Java 17+ DSL (`dev.pathland.view`):
declarative views, Angular-style signals, fine-grained emitter, `PLPL` wire
codec, lazy JNA ring interop, and cross-platform `State`. Protocol contract:
`spec/`. Runs on every LTS from Java 17.

## Implemented

- **`ProxyView`** (`ProxyView.make(p -> p.endpoint(...).route(...).credential(...))`):
  a `PROXY_VIEW` (0x1E) container whose child subtree is served by **another**
  Pathland server (spec/PROXY.md). It authors **no** children — the origin root is
  spliced in at runtime — and takes size modifiers like any view. The immutable
  `ProxyConfig` snapshot rides the node (`PathlandNode.proxyConfig`) and is
  surfaced to the host through `RenderResult.proxyViews()` (node id → config) so
  `pathland-server-core` opens an origin connection per proxy node. The emitter's
  internal `onStructureReconciled(Runnable)` hook (like `snapshotEmission`) fires
  after each structural reconcile — after the routing maps reflect the new subtree
  — so the host reconciles origin connections against the live `proxyViews` map
  (a proxy lives exactly while its node is in the retained tree, spec/PROXY.md §7).
- **`SizeThatFits` fit slot** (`SizeThatFits.make(Fit...)` + `Fit.of(view, minWidth)`):
  a structural slot (`SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17) emitting `FIT_QUERY` (LIST, ascending
  thresholds) + the single selected child — unselected candidates never transmit.
  The host routes `FIT_CHANGED` into the slot's fit sink
  (`RenderResult.fitInputs`, via `InputDispatcher`), which swaps the child through
  the structural reconcile (an unchanged index re-emits zero opcodes). The LIST
  value type is written by `FrameOpcodeSink`/`RingOpcodeSink`
  (`[count][f32 × count]` arena entries). A slot's selection is **retained node
  state** (`PathlandNode.fitSelection`): a parent-subtree re-render (an outer
  slot's candidate swap, a custom style body re-run) may rebuild a nested slot
  with a default index, so the reconcile **carries the previous selection across
  the match** (`Emitter.restoreFitSelection`) — a nested fit (the player bar's
  controls slot under the root row) keeps its candidate instead of resetting to
  compact (a reset would strand the DOM client, which never re-reports an
  unchanged width). The **web-SSR full-snapshot emission** (issue #141) is an
  internal emitter mode (`Emitter.snapshotEmission(true)`, armed by
  `PathlandSession`): on mount/resync the slot emits EVERY candidate in `FIT_QUERY`
  order so the SSR renders all branches gated by CSS container queries (a no-JS
  correct first paint) — the authored DSL is unchanged. `PathlandNode.fitReported`
  gates the mount-time structural effect so the multi-candidate presentation is
  not collapsed before the renderer reports; the first `FIT_CHANGED` (recorded
  before the incoming index) downgrades the slot to the single selected child via
  the normal reconcile, and the web client unwraps the gated branches. The
  downgrade is a **clean N→1**: it keeps the SELECTED candidate's node as-is
  (retaining its id + subtree, zero churn) and removes the others — it never
  positionally diffs, because both candidates are frequently the same component
  and morphing the loser's node into the winner would relocate the winner into
  the SSR's loser wrapper and break the renderer's candidate-position CSS gate.
  **View reuse** (issue #159): the same `View` instance may not be the candidate
  of two `Fit`s — `SizeThatFits.make` rejects it (`IllegalStateException`), since
  it would be materialized once per candidate and leak shared state / ids.
  Sharing a subtree **inside** two distinct candidate roots stays allowed; every
  materialized copy gets a distinct node id. The emitter enforces the frame's
  **unique-node-id invariant** (spec/OPCODE.md §Frame Lifecycle) with
  `Emitter.duplicateIds` / a fail-loud guard at mount, resync, and after each
  structural reconcile, so an id-overriding pass (an identity-stable node pinning
  a playback key) can never silently corrupt an id-keyed consumer.
- **v2 authoring surface (complete)**: every concrete view exposes
  the three operations — values via the static `View.make(...)`
  (`make(Consumer<Config>)`, `make(value)` shortcuts, empty `make()`),
  `.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` (an **instance** operation — the `View` interface
  ships a `default View.modifiers(ViewModifier...)` so a bare `View` value
  (a style's `config.label()`, a `Color`, a `FitSlot`) applies modifiers too, and
---315
  **thread-safe** (all entry points synchronized) so a request/SSR-thread flush can
  never race the actor's mid-flush mutation of another session's pending effects.
  An effect that **throws during a flush is not permanently unsubscribed**: its
  pre-run producer edges are restored, so it retries on the next dependency change
  (a transient error can't silently kill a node's binding).
- **Emitter** (`emit`): mounts once, stable ids, node-level binding effects
  (a signal change re-emits only that node), `FrameOpcodeSink` /
  `RingOpcodeSink`. For the ring path, a bound `text`/`value`/`date` control
  carries `BINDING_ID` on **every** emission path — mount, a matched reconcile,
  and a newly created subtree — so a control materialized by a structural slot
  (e.g. the player bar's wide volume slider, created when its nested
  `SIZE_THAT_FITS` swaps) still reports `VALUE_CHANGED`; the frame/SSR sink
  omits the marker. **`Signals.constant` / `ConstantSignal`**: a view or
  modifier holds one `Signal<T>` per reactive value (the raw `of(T)` overload is
  sugar for a constant); the emitter treats a constant as a plain, non-reactive
  property (no binding/effect).
- **Structural reactivity** (spec DSL.md §3.4): `Conditional.when(Signal<Boolean>,
  then, else)` and `when(Signal<T>, Case.of(...)...) / Case.otherwise(...)` —
  statically importable lowercase factories on a final class (mirrors
  `Signals`; `if`/`switch`/`case`/`else` are Java keywords). A structural
  container materializes as a `Group` slot (bare `VSTACK` node); the emitter's
  structural effect reconciles the slot's single child on selector change —
  position+type-stable ids, `TREE` deltas only, identical recompute emits
  **zero** opcodes, nested containers work, and the slot's subtree owns its own
  bindings. `RenderResult` routing maps are now live unmodifiable views (a swap
  updates tap/text/value/date routing after mount).
- **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.router`, spec DSL.md §4.5): `Route` (absolute
  path, `pathOnly()` strips query/fragment), `RouteTable` (literal + `:param`
  patterns, guards → `replace()` redirect, `fallback` 404), `Router`
  (`Signal<Route>` + back-stack; `navigate`/`push`/`pop`/`replace`/`back`,
  `handlePlatformNavigation`/`handleEvent`), **`Navigation`** (the ergonomic
  facade: `Navigation.navigator(initialPath).route(...).fallback(...).build()`
  collapses table + router + seeding, `Navigation.container(router)` is the slot,
  `Navigation.isActive(router, path)` → a reactive `Signal<Boolean>` for
  active-route styling, `Navigation.ROUTER` = the `EnvironmentKey<Router>`),
  **`Params`** (typed path-param access — `get`/
  `intValue`/`longValue`/`doubleValue`/`booleanValue`/`path` — replacing the raw
  `Map` in `RouteHandler`), **a bound router** (`Navigation.navigator()...
  .build(WritableSignal<String>)` — the router binds to the host-provided
  `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` signal: external writes are re-routed **guard-aware**,
  its own navigation is mirrored back, the initial value is guard-processed), and
  **generic scoped environment values**
  (`EnvironmentKey`/`EnvironmentValues` + the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value
  (`environmentBinding(e -> e.key(key).value(value))`) +
  `Environment.value(key)` — the `.environment` style, hierarchical nearest-
  wins; a `NavigationContainer` scopes `Navigation.ROUTER` to its destination
  subtree and structural slots re-apply the incoming scope on re-render via
  `PathlandNode.environmentForChildren`/`Emitter.reconcileSlot`; **reads always
  return a signal** — `Environment.value(key)` → `Signal<T>`, a value injected as
  a `Signal` comes back as the same instance (bindable for reactive updates) and a
  plain value is wrapped in a constant signal; a read made before the key is bound
  returns a **lazy signal** that captures the binding on the first `.get()` during
  render, enabling the `@Environment` **field style**
  (`private final Signal<Router> router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER);`)),
---450
  On the ring (desktop) path the emitter auto-sets `BINDING_ID` for bound
  controls (see Implemented) — the GTK renderer gates value/text events on it.
- Structural reconcile does not emit `SET_PROPERTY` for a *removed* property on
  a matched node (the wire has no unset; the renderer keeps the last value) —
  consistent with the Rust engine.

# Pathland Structural Reactivity + Router — Implementation Plan

**Status:** Approved — in progress (Phases 0–3, 5a/5b/5c, 6 complete)
**Branch:** `feat/router-structural-reactivity`
**Last Updated:** September 8, 2026

---

## Goal

A cross-platform router for Pathland: browser-path parity (Angular Router /
react-router style) **and** native navigation compatibility (SwiftUI
NavigationStack, Jetpack Compose NavHost, WinUI NavigationView, LVGL screens),
built as a DSL-level construct that respects the protocol's non-negotiables:
stateless renderers, app-owned tree, diff-based emission, "WHAT never WHERE".

## Foundation-first design

**Conditional rendering (structural reactivity) is the reusable primitive.**
A structural container owns a subtree selected by a signal and reconciles it on
change, emitting `TREE` deltas. The router is a structural container whose
content function is route-table matching, plus router-specific extras
(back-stack, URL sync, the `NAVIGATE` event, the `ROUTE`/`TRANSITION`
properties).

parts.text:
The test custom views in `PathlandSessionTest` override `renderNode` and call `.render(env)` on the Text, creating a child slot whose node is returned by the custom view's renderNode. This is the aliasing issue: the custom view's slot node = Text child slot's node; two slots own the same node. Does this break? The full `mvn install` passed, including these tests. It may work because the child slot's node is the same as the parent slot's node; `linkSlots` sets `node.slot` to the child slot (set in renderView), overwriting the parent's `node.slot = slot`? In `renderView` for the parent custom view, after its renderNode returns the child node, we set `slot.node = node; node.slot = slot;` — this overwrites the child slot's ownership! The child slot's tracked effect still exists, and its `node` points to the same node with `slot = parent`. Then `walkOwned` for the parent will visit the node (slot == parent) and register bindings; the child slot also registers bindings for its node (slot == parent != child → `walkOwned` skips, so the child slot registers nothing). The child slot's tracked effect still runs on its reads and reconciles the node; its `node.slot` is parent. It may double-reconcile. In practice, the tests pass, but this is fragile. The DSL contract says a custom view that returns content should use `renderNode` (root chain) to avoid a child slot. The test should be updated to `.renderNode(env)` to follow the contract. But user code might do this. We could make `renderView` detect when the returned node already has a slot from a child slot created during this render, and in that case treat the parent slot as transparent (don't overwrite `node.slot`, and the parent slot delegates to the child slot). That would support custom views that call `.render(env)` for their root. Let's think:
- In `renderView`, after the initial value, if `node.slot != null` and `node.slot != slot` (the node was produced by a child slot during this render), then the parent view is a "pass-through" component: it doesn't own a node; its `node` is the child slot's node. We should not overwrite `node.slot`. The parent slot's tracked computation includes the view's body reads; on re-run, it re-renders and produces a fresh child node; `reconcileSlot(slot, fresh)` should reconcile the child slot's node, not `slot.node`. But `slot.node` would be the same as the child slot's node; the parent slot's `nodeParent/index` might not be set (linkSlots sets it for the node's slot, which is the child slot; the parent slot's nodeParent remains null). On re-run, `reconcileSlot` for the parent would think it's the root and fail. We could mark the parent slot as `passThrough = true` and, on re-run, delegate reconciliation to the fresh child slot? Complex.
- Simpler: keep the contract: custom views must use `renderNode` for their root chain. Update the two tests to `.renderNode(env)`; they still pass. Document in `View.renderNode` javadoc. The aliasing risk remains for non-conforming user code, but it's a POC and documented.
- Alternatively, make `View.render` fallback for direct calls outside an emitter call `renderNode`, which it does. In tests, the custom view's `renderNode` calls `Text.make(...).render(env)`; since an emitter is current, it creates a child slot. We can change the test to `.renderNode(env)`. Let's do that to keep the model clean.
- Search for other custom `renderNode` methods that call `.render(env)` on their root. `RouterTest` line 107: `node.children.add(child.render(env))` — that's a custom primitive building children, correct. Line 333/334: a custom view likely builds a VStack with children; `NavigationLink...render(env)` and `NavigationContainer...render(env)` as children of a node; correct (child slots). Line 668: `return Button.make(...).render(env)` inside a custom `renderNode` — pass-through; should be `renderNode`. `PathlandSessionTest` two. `rebuiltNested` we already changed.
- Let's update `RouterTest` line 668 and `PathlandSessionTest` to `.renderNode`. But are these tests asserting behavior that might change? The pass-through view's root is the Text/Button; using `renderNode` keeps it in the same slot, which is the intended component. Should still pass.
- Also search for `return ... .render(env)` in tests. Use grep.

parts.text:
Now let's inspect the git diff to ensure no accidental issues, and check `git status`. Also we should consider the `RenderContext`/`Emitter.current` thread-local and the `Effect` flush behavior with SSR/actor threads. The full server tests pass, so good.

Potential remaining issues:
1. `Emitter.current()` static ThreadLocal is set during `renderView` and `renderSlot`; but the tracked effect's `onRecompute` (`reconcileSlot`) runs inside the effect context. The `renderSlot` supplier installs CURRENT. Good.
2. The `Signals.tracked` effect's first run may be queued; when it runs, it calls `computed.get()` which runs `renderSlot` (installs CURRENT). Good.
3. `reconcileSlot` calls `registerSlotTree` which creates node-level effects. Those effects are created inside the slot's tracked effect (when reconcileSlot is called by the tracked effect). `Signals.effect` schedules them; since we're inside a flush, they queue and run after. Good. The old emitter did the same in `reconcileSlot`.
4. `destroySlotBindings(slot)` is called at the start of `reconcileSlot`; it destroys node-level effects. If one of those effects is currently running (the slot tracked effect is not in slot.bindings), fine.
5. `reconcileSnapshotFit` calls `registerSlotBindings(slot)` and `collectSlotInputs(slot, null)`. It doesn't re-register the keep child slot's bindings (they remain). Good. But it calls `collectSlotInputs(slot, null)` which recurses into `slot.children` (keepSlot) and re-collects its inputs with `enclosing=null`; if the keep subtree has a NavigationContainer router, `collectOwnedInputs` will find it. Fine. It doesn't overwrite `navigateHandler`? `refreshNavigateHandler` after. Good.
6. `reconcileSnapshotFit` calls `destroySlotBindings(slot)` and `forgetSlotInputs(slot)` before the special case? In `reconcileSlot`, we moved `destroySlotBindings(slot)`/`forgetSlotInputs(slot)` before the special-case check. Yes. `destroySlotBindings(slot)` walks `slot.node` (old FitSlot node) and skips child slots, removing FitSlot node bindings (none). `forgetSlotInputs(slot)` removes FitSlot node inputs (fitInput). Then `reconcileSnapshotFit` calls `collectSlotInputs(slot, null)` which re-adds the FitSlot node's fitInput (fresh node) and recurses into keepSlot. Good.
7. `reconcileSnapshotFit` destroys `newChildren` (the fresh selected candidate child slot). But the fresh node `fresh.children` is cleared and set to `keep`; the destroyed child slot's node is discarded. Good.
8. `reconcileSnapshotFit` sets `old.children` to [keep]; this mutates the old retained node. The `dropOps` remove the other candidates. The `keep` node remains in the renderer. The fresh FitSlot node's `children` [keep]; `reconcileNode(old, fresh)` compares old [keep] vs fresh [keep] → zero. Good.
9. `slot.node = fresh`; `slot.children` = [keepSlot]; `linkSlots(fresh)` updates keepSlot's nodeParent/index. Good.
10. `reconcileSnapshotFit` does not set `fresh.fitSelection`? The fresh node's `fitSelection` was set in render. Good.
11. `fitInput` wrapper in `collectInputsForNode` sets `snapshotActive=false` before `inner.accept(index)`. Good.
12. The `snapshotActive` flag is set at mount from `snapshotEmission`; it stays true until a fit report. For non-SSR apps (`snapshotEmission=false`), it's false from mount, so FitSlots render single candidate. Good.
13. `renderSlot` sets `PathlandNode.SNAPSHOT_EMISSION.set(snapshotActive)` for every slot render. For a non-fit component, harmless. For a FitSlot re-render before first fit in SSR, it renders all candidates (snapshotActive true). Good. After first fit, false.
14. `renderFull` replays `tree`; after a body re-render before first fit, the tree remains snapshot (because snapshotActive true). Good.
15. `SizeThatFits` hint: `Emitter.currentSlotOldFitSelection()` uses `renderStack.peek()` (the FitSlot slot) and `slot.oldNodeHint`; we clear `oldNodeHint` after the first render. Good. On a parent re-render, a fresh FitSlot slot gets `oldNodeHint` from `oldChildHint(parent, index)`. We use `parent.node != null ? parent.node : parent.oldNodeHint`. For a fresh parent slot (node null), use its oldNodeHint (the old parent node). Good.
16. The `oldChildHint` index uses `parent.renderingChildren.size()` before adding the child slot. This assumes the child slot order matches the old node's children order. For most primitives, yes. The nested test passes. Good enough for POC; document? Maybe mention in status/DSL? Not necessary.
17. `View.of` supplier returning null: `ReactiveSlotView` handles null (no child). The slot's node is a Group VSTACK; stable. Good.
18. Root stability: `reconcileSlot` throws if root component changes. The test covers. Good.
19. Non-signal read: test covers.
20. Modifiers: test covers via renderFull. Good.
21. Environment scope: test covers.
22. Media/State: existing tests pass.

One concern: `Text.renderNode` now uses `Signals.untracked(config.binding()::get)`. If the binding is a `ConstantSignal`, untracked is fine. If the binding is a computed, it's evaluated untracked (the computed's own deps recorded). The node binding effect later reads it tracked. Good.

Another concern: `PathlandNode.property` now uses `ReactiveValues.initial` (untracked). This is used in `VStack`/`HStack` etc. for alignment/spacing signals. If a spacing signal is reactive, the node-level binding effect (`node.propertyBindings`? Wait, `PathlandNode.property(id, signal)` sets `properties` and, if not constant, `propertyBindings.put(id, signal)`. The binding effect will track it. The initial read is untracked. Good.
- `Modified` uses `ReactiveValues.initial` and then `node.propertyBindings.put`; good.
- `Toggle` style uses `node.property(TOGGLE_STYLE, constant)`; untracked constant. Fine.
- `ColorPicker`/Slider/Icon/Image/Toggle initial values untracked. Good.

What about `Button.renderNode` reading `env.buttonStyle()` which reads a signal via `Environment.value(BUTTON_STYLE).get()`. If the style is a constant signal, no subscription. If a reactive style signal, the button component subscribes and re-renders on style change. That's arguably correct. But it could also cause a body re-render on every environment style signal change; rare. Fine.

What about `Label`/`Icon` etc. reading environment styles? Same.

What about `Video`/`MediaController`? `materializeControllers` is untracked in mount? In mount, it's called outside a tracked render, so no subscription. In `reconcileSlot`, wrapped in untracked. Good. But `Video.renderNode` may read `controller` signals? Let's check. It sets `node.mediaControllerRef` and maybe `node.properties.put(MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID?)`. It likely doesn't read. Existing tests pass.

Now, a critical semantic: the per-component slot's tracked computation uses `Signals.tracked` with `ComputedSignal` equality `Objects.equals`. For `PathlandNode` values, identity inequality → effect runs. Good. But the `Tracked` effect's first run is queued when created inside a flush. Suppose a slot is created during a parent re-render, and its child effect's first run is queued. The parent re-render's `reconcileSlot` calls `registerSlotTree`, which registers node-level effects for the fresh nodes. Those effects are also queued. The child slot's tracked effect first run runs after the parent effect; it reads the computed (cached) and sets first=false. But the child slot's `node` was already set in `renderView` from `tracked.initial()`. Good.
- If a signal changes between the parent render and the child effect's first run (within the same flush? Signals could be set by a node-level effect that runs before the child effect). The child effect's first run would read the computed; if the computed is dirty (a dependency changed), it re-evaluates and calls `onRecompute`? The effect body checks `first[0]` and returns without calling `onRecompute`, but the computed re-evaluated and its value changed; the child slot's node is stale (the initial value), and no reconcile happens because first run skipped. This is a subtle bug: if a dependency changes before the child tracked effect's first run, the re-evaluation happens during the first run, but `onRecompute` is skipped due to `first` flag, so the slot doesn't reconcile the changed value.
  - How likely? A signal write during the same flush before the child effect's first run. For example, a parent re-render creates a child slot; a node-level binding effect (registered earlier) writes a signal that the child reads; the child effect's first run sees the change but skips reconcile. This could cause stale UI until the next change.
  - Fix: In `Signals.tracked`, the effect's first run should distinguish "first run, value unchanged from initial" vs "first run, value changed". We can compare the computed value to the initial value:
    ```java
    T initial = untracked(computed::get);
    T[] last = { initial };
    boolean[] first = {true};
    EffectRef effect = effect(() -> {
        T value = computed.get();
        if (first[0]) {
            first[0] = false;
            if (value != initial && !Objects.equals(value, initial)) {
                onRecompute.accept(value);
            }
            return;
        }
        onRecompute.accept(value);
    });
    ```
    - If the value changed before the first effect run, `value` != initial → call onRecompute. If unchanged, skip. This handles the race.
    - For `PathlandNode` values, `value != initial` (identity) even if the computed re-evaluated to a fresh node with the same content. But if the computed re-evaluated, the value is a fresh node (different identity) even if content same; calling onRecompute would diff and emit zero ops (fine). If the computed did not re-evaluate (cached), `value == initial` (same object) → skip. Good.
    - Use `Objects.equals` plus identity. `value != initial` is enough for PathlandNode; for value types, `Objects.equals`.
  - Let's update `Signals.tracked` accordingly. This is important for correctness.
  - Also, `ComputedSignal` equality suppression: if the value is equal, it keeps the cached object; `value == initial`. Good.
- Another subtlety: `Tracked.initial()` returns the initial value; the slot uses it. If the effect's first run changes and calls `onRecompute`, the slot's `node` is set to initial before the effect runs; `reconcileSlot` will reconcile the fresh value against initial. But `reconcileSlot` requires `slot.node` set and `slot.nodeParent`/`nodeIndex` linked. During the parent re-render, the child slot's `nodeParent`/`nodeIndex` are not linked until the parent's `reconcileSlot` calls `linkSlots` after the diff. If the child effect's first run (queued after the parent effect) calls `reconcileSlot` and `slot.nodeParent` is null, it would throw stable-root error or set `this.tree`. Hmm. The child effect runs after the parent effect completes; the parent `reconcileSlot` calls `linkSlots(fresh)` before returning, so the child slot's nodeParent/index are set. Then the child effect's first run runs and can reconcile. Good. If the child effect is created during the parent's first render (mount), the parent's mount calls `linkSlots(tree)` after `root.render` returns, before the effect flush? `root.render` creates the root tracked; `Signals.tracked` initial evaluation runs the root supplier, creating child slots and their effects. The child effects' first runs are queued or immediate? `Signals.tracked` for the child calls `effect(...)`, which flushes immediately if not already flushing. During the root supplier (inside `untracked(computed::get)`), is a flush in progress? The root `Signals.tracked` first evaluates the computed in `untracked` (no effect yet); then creates the root effect, which schedules/flushes. The root effect's body reads the computed (cached) and sets first=false. The child effects were created during the root computed evaluation (before the root effect), and each `effect(...)` flushed immediately (no flush in progress). So child effects run before `root.render` returns and before `linkSlots`. If a child effect's first run detects a changed value and calls `reconcileSlot`, `slot.nodeParent` is null (not linked yet) → bug. The race is possible if a signal changes during the child render (e.g., a body writes a signal—not allowed—or a node-level effect? Node-level effects are registered after mount). During mount, no signal writes should happen. So the race is unlikely at mount. During a parent re-render, the parent effect is flushing; child effects are queued; the parent `reconcileSlot` links before the child effects run. So the race is handled. The `first` value-change fix is still good for robustness.
  - To be safe, `reconcileSlot` could check if `slot.nodeParent == null && slot.node != this.tree` (not the root slot) and defer? But that complicates. The main scenario is covered.
  - Let's update `Signals.tracked` for the first-run change.

Also, another subtlety: `Signals.tracked` creates a `ComputedSignal` and an `Effect`. The effect's first run may be queued; if the slot is destroyed before the first run, the effect is destroyed. Fine.

Let me update `Signals.tracked`.

I see `markFitReported()` is unused now; we clear `snapshotActive` in `collectInputsForNode` wrapper. Remove `markFitReported` to avoid dead code. Also `snapshotEmission` field is used in mount. Fine.

Potential bug in `reconcileSnapshotFit`: `destroySlotBindings(slot)`/`forgetSlotInputs(slot)` were already called before the special case. Good. But `reconcileSnapshotFit` doesn't call `destroySlotBindings(slot)` again; it calls `registerSlotBindings(slot)` and `collectSlotInputs(slot, null)`. The FitSlot node's fitInput was forgotten and re-collected. Good.
- `oldChildren` may include child slots that are not in `old.children`? They should correspond. `keepSlot = keep.slot`. Good.
- `newChildren` fresh selected candidate slot is destroyed; but `slot.children` is set to [keepSlot]. Good.
- `fresh.children` [keep]; `keep.slot` is keepSlot; `linkSlots(fresh)` updates keepSlot.nodeParent/index. Good.
- `fresh.id = old.id`; `old.children` [keep]; `reconcileNode(old, fresh)` compares properties and children. Good.

One issue: in the general `reconcileSlot`, we call `destroySlotBindings(slot)` and `forgetSlotInputs(slot)` **before** checking the special case, but we do not destroy the old **child slots** before the special case (the special case destroys them selectively). Good.
- However, for the general case, `destroySlotBindings(slot)` walks `slot.node` (old) and removes nodeBindings for owned nodes; then we destroy old child slots. Fine.
- For the general case, `forgetSlotInputs(slot)` removes inputs for owned nodes; child slots handle theirs. Then we destroy old child slots (forget their inputs). Good.
- For the root slot, `slot.nodeParent == null`; if component same, reconcile; if different, throw. Good.
- For a child slot whose component changes, we remove/delete old at parent index, create/insert fresh. But we also need to destroy the old child slots of the slot (done) and set `slot.children` to new. Good.
- `emitSubtreeInto` emits all properties for the fresh subtree, including child slot nodes. But those child slots' own tracked effects/bindings are registered later. Fine.
- `fresh.id = freshIdFor(fresh)`; `emitSubtreeInto` assigns fresh ids to children. Good.
- `slot.nodeParent.children.set(slot.nodeIndex, fresh)` assumes the parent's children list has old at index. Good.

Potential issue: `reconcileNode(old, fresh, ops)` for a matched component but `fresh` has a different number of children; `reconcileChildren` handles create/delete. Good.

Potential issue: `destroySlotBindings(slot)` removes `nodeBindings` entries for the slot's owned nodes. If a node is matched and reused, its node bindings are destroyed and re-registered by `registerSlotTree`. Good.
- But `destroySlotBindings(slot)` is called before the diff; it walks `slot.node` (old). For a composite slot whose node is a child slot's node? We set `node.slot = slot` for the composite's returned node, so the composite slot owns it. The child slot that produced it may also exist? In our model, a composite's `renderNode` delegates via `renderNode` to the resolved view, so no child slot for the root; the composite slot owns the node. Good. Custom views that call `.render(env)` create a child slot and then the parent overwrites `node.slot = slot`; the child slot still exists but is skipped by `walkOwned` (node.slot == parent != child) and its tracked effect remains. This is the aliasing issue we documented; we updated tests to `renderNode`. For user code, it's a risk. We could detect and throw a clear error in `renderView` if the returned node already has a slot different from this slot (indicating a pass-through custom view). That would enforce the contract loudly. But it might break existing apps/tests. Since the tests are updated and the contract is documented, we can add a check:
  ```java
  if (node.slot != null && node.slot != slot) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("a view's renderNode must use renderNode (not render) for its root content ...");
  }
  ```
  This would catch the aliasing early. But `node.slot` for a child slot's node is set to the child slot. If the parent view returned that node directly, we'd throw. That's good. However, `View.render` fallback for direct calls outside an emitter doesn't set slots; no issue. Let's add this check in `renderView` after `tracked.initial()`:
  ```java
  if (node != null && node.slot != null && node.slot != slot) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("View " + view.getClass().getName() + " returned a node owned by a child slot; use renderNode(env) for root-chain delegation");
  }
  ```
  But there's a case where a custom view intentionally returns a child view's node (pass-through) and wants the child slot to own it. Our model can't support it; throwing is honest. The two tests we updated would have thrown. Good. Should we add it? It might catch real app code (demos use body/renderNode; likely fine). The full tests pass without it; adding it is a safety net. Let's add.
- Also remove `markFitReported` unused.

Another potential issue: `currentSlotOldFitSelection()` is public; it's emitter-internal but `SizeThatFits` calls it. Fine.

Let's add the aliasing check and remove unused method.

parts.text:
The test `aRetainedNodeReusedAcrossCandidatesTripsTheUniqueIdGuard` expects the duplicate-id guard message, but our aliasing check fires first. The custom view returns a cached `PathlandNode` that is reused across candidates; `node.slot` is set to the first slot, then the second candidate's render returns the same node with `node.slot` = first slot → our check throws a different message. The test expects "duplicate node id". We could relax the check: only throw if the node's slot is a **child slot created during this render**, not any other slot. We can detect by checking if the node's slot is in `slot.renderingChildren` (the child slots created during this render). For the cached node case, the node's slot is a slot from a previous render/candidate, not in the current `renderingChildren`. For the pass-through case, the node's slot is a child slot created during this render and is in `slot.renderingChildren`. Let's implement:
```java
if (node.slot != null && node.slot != slot && slot.renderingChildren != null && slot.renderingChildren.contains(node.slot)) {
    throw ...
}
```
This catches the pass-through case but allows the cached-node duplicate-id test to proceed to the duplicate-id guard. Good.
- `renderingChildren` contains the child slots created during this slot's render. The pass-through custom view calls `.render(env)` which creates a child slot and adds it to the parent slot's `renderingChildren`; then the parent returns that child's node. The node's slot is in `renderingChildren` → throw. Good.
- The cached node reused across candidates: the node's slot is from a previous candidate slot (not in the current `renderingChildren`), so no throw; the duplicate-id guard catches it later. Good.
- At mount, `guardUniqueIds` runs before? In mount, `assignIds` then `linkSlots` then `materializeControllers` then `guardUniqueIds`. The cached node is reused across candidates: the first candidate's render sets `node.slot = slot1`; the second candidate's render returns the same node; our check sees `node.slot = slot1` not in `slot2.renderingChildren` → no throw. Then `assignIds` assigns the same node id twice? `assignIds` walks the tree and assigns ids; the cached node appears twice; `nextFreeId` gives different ids on each visit, but it's the same object, so the last assignment wins; `duplicateIds` detects the duplicate. The test passes. Good.

- Or `VStack.children(List<View>)` overload accepting a `List<View>` (currently varargs). The loop still builds the list.

- Or use `IntStream.range(...).mapToObj(...).toArray(View[]::new)` — more concise but still lambda, no explicit `ArrayList`/index capture.

Given the new per-component reactive body model, we can also make a reactive list helper:

VStack.make().children(

        .track(track).index(i)...)));
```
But if `TRACKS` is static, no reactivity needed. If it's a `Signal<List<T>>`, the helper should be a component (`View.of`-like) that reads the signal and re-renders rows. That would be a nice DSL addition.

No ForEach helper. The user's question is about code style/DSL ergonomics. We should propose options, likely a new `ForEach`/`View.forEach` helper. Given plan mode, we need to present a plan, ask clarifying questions.

Let me think about the best design:

Option 1: Add a `ForEach` DSL component:
```java
public final class ForEach {
    public static <T> View of(List<T> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content)
    public static <T> View of(Signal<List<T>> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content) // reactive
}
```
Usage:
```java
VStack.make().children(
    ForEach.of(MusicPlayerView.TRACKS, (track, i) -> TrackRowView.make(r -> r
        .track(track).index(i)...)));
```
- The static list version maps once (at render) to a Group/VStack of children.
- The signal version is a component whose tracked render reads the signal and maps; it re-renders rows on list change. But list diffing is position+type (no keys), so reordering churns; document.
- Could be a `View` itself, so it can be a child of a container. It would create a Group wrapper (VSTACK) like `View.of`, adding a node. Or it could return a `View[]`/`List<View>` for `.children(...)`. Since `.children(View...)` accepts varargs, a `ForEach` that returns `View[]` could be used:
  ```java
  VStack.make().children(ForEach.views(TRACKS, (t,i) -> ...))
  ```
  But `children(View...)` takes varargs; a `View[]` works. A `ForEach.views` returning `View[]` is simple and doesn't add a wrapper node. But for reactive lists, you need a component (wrapper node) to track the signal. Two APIs:
  - `ForEach.views(Iterable<T>, BiFunction<T,Integer,View>) -> View[]` for static lists (no wrapper).
  - `ForEach.of(Signal<List<T>>, BiFunction<T,Integer,View>) -> View` for reactive lists (Group wrapper).
  Or a single `ForEach` component that always wraps; simpler API but adds a node.

Option 2: Add a `children` overload accepting `List<View>`/`Iterable<View>`:
```java
public ViewBuilder<...> children(List<? extends View> children)
```
Then the loop still builds a `List<View>`, but you can use a stream:
```java
List<View> rows = IntStream.range(0, TRACKS.size())
    .mapToObj(i -> TrackRowView.make(...))
    .toList();
```
Still verbose. Could add `children(Collection<View>)` and a `View.map` helper.

Option 3: Add `View.forEach` / `Views.map` static:
```java
public static <T> List<View> map(List<T> items, BiFunction<T,Integer,View> fn)
```
Usage:
```java
VStack.make().children(View.map(TRACKS, (track, i) -> TrackRowView.make(...)));
```
But `children` needs varargs; `List<View>` overload needed. Add both:
- `View.map(Iterable<T>, BiFunction<T,Integer,View>) -> List<View>`
- `ChildrenView.children(Collection<? extends View>)` overload on `ViewBuilder` (and maybe `View`?).
This avoids a wrapper node and is flexible. But it's not reactive for signal lists; for that, use `View.of(() -> ...)` or a `ForEach` component.

Option 4: Improve `TrackRowView` config to remove the index entirely:
- Add `Config.track(Track track)` that computes `index = MusicPlayerView.TRACKS.indexOf(track)`. Then the loop doesn't need `index` capture:
  ```java
  for (Track track : MusicPlayerView.TRACKS) {
      rows.add(TrackRowView.make(r -> r.track(track)...));
  }
  ```
  This is simpler and removes the `int index = i` capture. The index is derivable from the track. This is a demo-specific improvement, not a DSL feature. But it only simplifies the loop body, not the loop.

### The three operations

Every concrete view exposes the same three operations — **construction**
(`make`), **modifiers** (`.modifiers`), and **children** (`.children`). In the
Java realization `make(...)` **is the only static of the three**; a later call
overrides an earlier value for the same property.

| Operation | Purpose | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) |
|-----------|---------|----------------------------|
| **values** | Configure structural/layout values and a control's bound value | `View(config:)` — labels in the constructor |
| **modifiers** | Apply `ViewModifier` values, innermost-first | `.modifier(_:)` / `.padding(_:)` / … |
| **children** | Supply the content subtree (content-bearing views only) | trailing closure `{ … }` |

The **canonical builder spelling** (the recommended form; per-language spellings
are in [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)) is:

```
ViewName.make(values)              // values   — a config-builder lambda (Java views)
      .modifiers(modifier, ...)       // modifiers — varargs
      .children(view, ...)            // children  — varargs, content-bearing views only
```

In the Java realization a view's values entry is the static `make(...)` (the
construction factory; empty `make()` for config-less or value-less starts).
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation available on the builder and on any
`View` value (the interface default), so it (and `children(...)`) chain on the
builder in any order:

```
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).children(a, b).modifiers(m)
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).modifiers(m).children(a, b)
VStack.make().modifiers(m).children(a, b)
```

The old static `X.modifiers(...)` first-call entry points are **removed** —
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation (interface default for bare `View`
values, covariant override on the builder). Static `X.children(...)` is **kept**
as a value-less first-call convenience (`HStack.children(a, b)` ≡
`HStack.make().children(a, b)`); `make(...)` is the only values static.

**Values are a config-builder lambda.** `make { c in … }` populates a per-view
fluent **config** (`VStack.Config`, `Text.Config`, …). It is the *same type* a
style's `makeBody(Config)` receives ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
The builder is **fluent and mutable**: setters return the config. Config-less
views (`Divider`, `Spacer`) take an empty `make()`.

**Every value member is reactive-capable (MUST).** A config member that carries a
value exposes **two forms** — a raw value and a `Signal<T>`:

```
Text.make(t -> t.text("hi"))            ≡  Text.make(t -> t.text(constant("hi")))
visible(v -> v.visible(flagSignal))      // reactive visibility
frame(f -> f.width(widthSignal))         // reactive sizing, layout included
```

The **raw form is sugar for a constant signal**; a **non-constant** signal
becomes a **node-level binding** — a change re-emits only that node's `SET_TEXT`
/ `SET_PROPERTY`, and a constant emits as a plain property with **zero binding
overhead**. This holds for *every* value member, layout included
(`spacing`, `alignment`, `padding`, `frame`, `columns`, …): anything describable
in the protocol can animate. A control's two-way *value* takes a
`WritableSignal<T>`; every other member takes a one-way `Signal<T>`.

**Per-language realization.** Java cannot declare a static and an instance
method with the same signature, so the Java realization holds the values entry
**statically** (`make(...)`) and exposes the chainable forms on the returned
builder/view type — `.modifiers(...)` is an instance operation (a `View`
interface default, covariantly overridden on the builder), and static
`X.children(...)` is retained as a value-less first-call convenience. Other
languages map the operations to their idioms (extension methods, associated
functions + traits, package constructors + methods, kwargs) — see [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules).

**Single-value shortcuts.** A view or modifier whose config designates a
**primary value member** MAY also expose a single-value construction overload that
is pure sugar for the config-builder lambda (views construct with `make(value)`,
modifiers with the lowercase function's value form):
---
1. **Names**: SwiftUI view/modifier names; per-language case (camelCase,
   snake_case). `foregroundStyle` not `foregroundColor`; `fontWeight`,
   `multilineTextAlignment`, `scaledToFit`, `allowsHitTesting` keep their
   SwiftUI spellings. A modifier's type is **never** suffixed `Mod`.

   `.border(color, width)`, `.frame(width, height, alignment)`,
   `.shadow(color, radius, x, y)`. Compound modifiers expand to one property
   per argument.
3. **Values vs modifiers**: structural/layout values and a control's bound value
   are configured through a view's `make(...)` (modifiers through lowercase
   functions); everything else is a chainable `modifiers(...)` value. The three
   operations may be chained in any order.
4. **Typed enums**: `HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing, for
   `VStack`), `VerticalAlignment` (top/center/bottom, for `HStack`), `Alignment`
   (2D — topLeading … bottomTrailing — for `ZStack`/grids and the `frame`
   modifier's content alignment); all **position-only, never stretching** (a
   child's `FILL` size kind stretches). Plus `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight`

   `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
   `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
   `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
   (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
   `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
   (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
   come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer` is a flexible expanding filler;
   `Color` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
6. **The environment is the only inheritance mechanism.** Any value that must
   reach a whole subtree — a style (`ButtonStyle`), the router, the active path,
   the session's persisted state — is injected through the environment, never
   threaded through constructors and never through a second scoping system. The
   environment is a hierarchical, nearest-wins scope of typed `EnvironmentKey`
   values (the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value / `Environment.value(key)`,
   Java; §4.5). A language MAY implement the scope with a thread-local over the
   synchronous render pass (Java does) — but that is the implementation of the
   one mechanism, not an additional one. A subtree-scoping modifier MUST be
   expressed as an `EnvironmentKey` binding: `ButtonStyle` binds
   `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` (`EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`), exactly like the
   router and the active path.
7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is a tracked render; a signal read there
   subscribes the component and a later write re-renders that component, whose
   subtree is diffed into deltas. A bound node stays fine-grained (one delta, no
   body re-run). Never write signals during render. Non-signal reads are
   mount-time only ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
   properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
   computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.

3. **Values vs modifiers**: structural/layout values and a control's bound value
   are configured through a view's `make(...)` (modifiers through lowercase
   functions); everything else is a chainable `modifiers(...)` value. The three
   operations may be chained in any order.
4. **Typed enums**: `HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing, for
   `VStack`), `VerticalAlignment` (top/center/bottom, for `HStack`), `Alignment`
   (2D — topLeading … bottomTrailing — for `ZStack`/grids and the `frame`
   modifier's content alignment); all **position-only, never stretching** (a
   child's `FILL` size kind stretches). Plus `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight`
   (100–900), `Truncation` (head/middle/tail),
   `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
   `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
   `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
   (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
   `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
   (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
   come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer` is a flexible expanding filler;
   `Color` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
6. **The environment is the only inheritance mechanism.** Any value that must
   reach a whole subtree — a style (`ButtonStyle`), the router, the active path,
   the session's persisted state — is injected through the environment, never
   threaded through constructors and never through a second scoping system. The
   environment is a hierarchical, nearest-wins scope of typed `EnvironmentKey`
   values (the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value / `Environment.value(key)`,
   Java; §4.5). A language MAY implement the scope with a thread-local over the
   synchronous render pass (Java does) — but that is the implementation of the
   one mechanism, not an additional one. A subtree-scoping modifier MUST be
   expressed as an `EnvironmentKey` binding: `ButtonStyle` binds
   `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` (`EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`), exactly like the
   router and the active path.
7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is a tracked render; a signal read there
   subscribes the component and a later write re-renders that component, whose
   subtree is diffed into deltas. A bound node stays fine-grained (one delta, no
   body re-run). Never write signals during render. Non-signal reads are
   mount-time only ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
   properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
   computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.

---

## 7. Theme management

Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
§Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:

# Pathland TypeScript View + Server — Implementation Plan

**Status:** Implemented (phases 1–6); phase 7 is the next follow-up
**Scope:** TypeScript-only, server-driven UI
**Last Updated:** October 22, 2026

---

## Goal

Build a TypeScript authoring and server runtime for Pathland:

- Angular-like developer experience: class views, decorators, callable signals,
  computed/effects, forced-once `body(props)`, fluent modifiers.
- The application runs on the server. The server owns the retained tree,
  signals, state, and session lifecycle.
- The browser hydrates SSR HTML and applies deltas. It does **not** run the
  view engine in this phase.
- SSR is rendered by the existing Rust `pathland-render-html` crate compiled to
  WebAssembly.
- The browser client is the existing `lib/typescript` `@pathland/dom-renderer`.
- Rust remains the source of truth for wire constants/conformance and the HTML
  renderer. Rust is not the runtime engine.

## Locked decisions

| Decision | Choice |
|---|---|
| Language | TypeScript only |
| AssemblyScript | Out of scope; no `view-as`, no closure transform, no dual-target |
| DX | Angular-like: class views, `@view`, callable signals, `body(props)`, modifiers |
| View restrictions | None from AS: optional props, closures, unions, and full TS are allowed |
| Execution model | Server-owned app; browser is a renderer |
| Browser runtime | Deferred; same TS engine must stay worker-compatible later |
| SSR | Rust `pathland-render-html` via a small wasm wrapper |
| Client | Reuse `lib/typescript` `@pathland/dom-renderer` |
| Server host | Node first; framework-agnostic core; Bun/Deno later |
| State | In-memory now; Redis interface documented and deferred |
| Context | Small `AppContext` (state/platform/route); no full Angular DI |
| Structural reactivity | Later; the reference view is static |
| Wire format | Existing 16-byte opcodes + PLPL batches, protocol v1 |

### Why not the alternatives

- **AssemblyScript / wasm app runtime:** rejected for this phase. It forces an
  AS-native DSL and a closure transform, sacrificing the Angular-like DX.
- **Rust engine runtime:** rejected. A TS app on Node would need per-call FFI;
  a non-Node host would need an embedded JS runtime. The TS engine is the future
  browser/worker runtime anyway.
- **A separate TS HTML serializer:** rejected as the primary path. Reuse the
  Rust HTML renderer for parity with the existing renderers.

## Non-goals

- No AssemblyScript compiler, transform, or runtime.
- No TS/AS byte-identity work.
- No SharedArrayBuffer ring, transferable double buffering, or worker DOM
  patcher.
- No browser-side application runtime in this phase.
- No Rust `pathland-engine` runtime dependency.
- No full Angular DI container, router, or zone.js.
- No structural/conditional rendering in phase 1; plan it as a follow-up.

---

## Architecture

```text
TypeScript view + engine (server)
        │
        ├── PLPL snapshot / delta batches
        │        ├── Rust pathland-render-html (WASM) → SSR HTML
        │        └── WebSocket → existing @pathland/dom-renderer
        │
        └── raw EVENT batches ← WebSocket ← browser
```

### Server flow

1. **SSR request**
   - Create a throwaway session with a random state scope.
   - Instantiate the app, connect state, mount the root view once.
   - Emit a full snapshot batch.
   - Render it with the Rust HTML wasm renderer.
   - Inject `data-pathland-base` and the content-hashed client bundle.
   - Close the throwaway session.
2. **WebSocket connect**
   - Client URL: `<base>/ws?wid=<window-id>`.
   - Register a pending session. The first message is `META::ENVIRONMENT`.
   - Create the live session with the `wid` state scope.
   - Do not re-send the mount frame; the client already has the SSR HTML.
3. **Deltas**
   - Signal changes emit only the affected opcodes.
   - Send monotonic PLPL batches when the connection is open.
   - `META::RESYNC` re-emits the full tree.
   - `META::PING` → `META::PONG`.
4. **Events**
   - Client sends raw EVENT batches.
   - The server updates bound signals; the engine emits deltas.
5. **Persistence**
   - Load `StateStore` values before mount.
   - Save on `State` changes.
   - Memory store now; Redis later.

---

## Repository layout

```text
lib/typescript/
├── package.json          # @pathland/dom-renderer + pnpm workspace root scripts
├── pnpm-workspace.yaml
├── pnpm-lock.yaml
├── tsconfig.base.json
├── src/                  # existing browser DOM client
├── packages/
│   ├── protocol/         @pathland/protocol
│   ├── signals/          @pathland/signals
│   ├── state/            @pathland/state
│   ├── view/             @pathland/view
│   ├── engine/           @pathland/engine
│   ├── ssr/              @pathland/ssr
│   └── server/           @pathland/server
└── examples/
    ├── profile-card/
    └── music-player/

lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html-wasm/   # new wasm wrapper
```

The existing `lib/typescript` package is both the browser client and the root
of the TypeScript server workspace. The browser client itself is not a
workspace member (it is the root package).

### Package dependency direction

```text
protocol
signals
  └── state
        └── view
              └── engine
                    └── server
                          ├── lib/typescript/examples/profile-card
                          └── lib/typescript/examples/music-player

protocol
  └── ssr
```

No circular dependencies. `engine` imports neither DOM nor Node APIs.

---

## Package contracts

### `@pathland/protocol`

```text
lib/typescript/packages/protocol/src/
  constants.ts   # generated from Rust pathland-ts-codegen
  batch.ts       # PLPL BatchWriter / BatchReader
  events.ts      # EVENT + META decode
  index.ts
```

```ts
export interface Opcode {
  category: number;
  command: number;
  flags: number;
  a: number;
  b: number;
  c: number;
}

export class BatchWriter {
  begin(): void;
  push(category: number, command: number, flags: number, a: number, b: number, c: number): void;
  string(value: string): number;  // arena offset
  end(sequence: number): Uint8Array;
}

export interface EventOpcode extends Opcode {
  text?: string;
}

export function decodeEvents(bytes: Uint8Array): EventOpcode[];
```

- Reuse the PLPL header/opcode/string layout already parsed by
  `lib/typescript/src/plpl.ts`.
- Use the existing implementation packing:
  `B = (valueType << 16) | propertyId`.
- F32 values are stored as raw IEEE-754 bits.
- Strings are length-prefixed UTF-8 in the batch string section.

### `@pathland/signals`

```text
lib/typescript/packages/signals/src/
  signal.ts
  computed.ts
  effect.ts
  input.ts
  index.ts
```

```ts
export interface ReadonlySignal<T> {
  (): T;
  get(): T;
}

export interface WritableSignal<T> extends ReadonlySignal<T> {
  set(value: T): void;
  update(fn: (current: T) => T): void;
}

export type MaybeSignal<T> = T | ReadonlySignal<T>;

parts.text:
The TS plan uses functions with props objects and children arrays/functions, not a `make` builder. That's important for cross-language design: TypeScript is "native" with functions and props objects; Java uses `make` builders; Kotlin could use builders or functions; Rust uses structs/builders.

The user's question: "What would you suggest if I wanted something recognizable across DSL's for rust, java, kotlin and typescript and stay as native to the language as possible?"

We need to propose a cross-language design convention. Given the repo's spec already has a "canonical SwiftUI-shaped" surface and per-language adaptation rules, the answer should align with that: a shared **conceptual vocabulary** and **semantic contract**, with idiomatic syntax per language. The recognizable parts should be:
- The **component render function** (`body()` / `build()` / `body(props)`).
- **Signals** (read = subscribe) with the same names (`signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`).
- **Native control flow** for branches: Java `if`/`switch` in body; Kotlin `if`/`when` expressions; Rust `if`/`match`; TypeScript ternary/`switch`.
- **List rendering**: a common `ForEach`/`each` concept for reactive lists; native `map`/`for` for static lists.
- **The three operations**: values/`make`, `modifiers`, `children` (or props/children functions in TS).
- **Component slots**: each child view is a component boundary; reads are local.

But "recognizable across DSLs" could mean the same API names. We should propose a **small canonical vocabulary** that each language spells idiomatically:
- `View`, `Text`, `VStack`, `HStack`, `Button`, etc. (same type names).
- `Signal`, `WritableSignal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked` (same names, case per language).
- `ForEach` (same name) for reactive lists; `View.of` (same name) for inline reactive subtrees; or use native expression forms where possible.
- `body`/`build` (same concept).
- `children`/`modifiers` (same names) where the language supports method chaining; TS can use props + children.
- `State`, `PersistentState`.

We should also warn against forcing identical syntax:
- Java: `make(...)`, `.modifiers(...)`, `.children(...)`, `View.of`, `ForEach.of`.
- Kotlin: `VStack(spacing = 8) { ... }` / `VStack.make { ... }` with trailing lambdas; `if`/`when` expressions; `items.mapIndexed { ... }` or `ForEach(items) { ... }`.
- Rust: `VStack::new(...).children(vec![...])`; `if`/`match`; `items.iter().enumerate().map(...)`; `ForEach::of(...)`.
- TypeScript: `VStack({ spacing: 8 }, [ ... ])`; `cond ? A : B`; `items.map((item, i) => ...)`; `ForEach(items, (item, i) => ...)`.

The common **recognizable** parts:
- Same conceptual names and semantics (the spec's canonical vocabulary).
- Same component/read model: reads subscribe the component.
- Same `ForEach`/`View.of` names for the non-native cases.
- Same wire semantics (diff, zero-op, etc.).

"Stay as native as possible" suggests:
- Don't force `View.of` in Kotlin/Rust/TS where `if`/`match`/ternary are expressions. Use the language's expression form directly.
- Don't force `ForEach` where native `map`/`for` suffices for static lists.
- Use `ForEach` only for reactive list scoping (or make it a helper that returns children).
- Use trailing lambdas (Kotlin), closures (Rust), arrow functions (TS), method chains (Java).
- Use language-specific case conventions (`snake_case` Rust, `camelCase` Java/TS/Kotlin).
- Use props objects in TS (native function components), builders in Java/Rust/Kotlin.

## Shared vocabulary (same everywhere)

- `View` / component render: `body()` (Java/Kotlin/TS), `build()` (Rust)
- `Signal`, `WritableSignal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`
- `State`, `PersistentState`
- `ForEach` — the named reactive-list helper
- `View.of` — the named inline reactive-subtree helper
- `children`, `modifiers`, values (`make` / `new` / props)

## Per-language spellings

| Concept | Java | Kotlin | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Component render | `View body()` | `View body()` | `fn build(&self)` | `body(props)` |
| Signal read | `sig.get()` | `sig.value` / `sig()` | `sig.get()` | `sig()` |
| Branch | `if`/`switch` in `body()`; `View.of(() -> …)` inline | `if`/`when` expressions | `if`/`match` expressions | ternary / `switch` expressions |
| Inline subtree | `View.of(() -> …)` | `View.of { … }` (rarely needed) | `View::of(\|\| …)` | `View.of(() => …)` |
| Static list | stream/`for` + `.children(...)` | `items.map { … }` + `.children(...)` | `items.iter().map(…)` + `.children(vec![…])` | `items.map(…)` + children array |
| Reactive list | `ForEach.of(items, (item, i) -> …)` | `ForEach(items) { item, i -> … }` | `ForEach::of(items, \|item, i\| …)` | `ForEach(items, (item, i) => …)` |
| Children | `.children(a, b)` | `.children(a, b)` / trailing lambda | `.children(vec![a, b])` | `children: [a, b]` / `() => [a, b]` |
| Values | `VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8))` | `VStack(spacing = 8)` / `make { … }` | `VStack::new(\|v\| v.spacing(8.0))` | `VStack({ spacing: 8 })` |
| Modifiers | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16.0))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` |

## Rules that keep it native and recognizable

1. **Use the language’s branch expression.** Java needs `View.of` for inline positions; Kotlin/Rust/TS do not. Don’t add a `Conditional` wrapper to languages that already have expression-level control flow.
2. **Use native iteration for static lists.** `map`/`for`/iterators are the idiomatic default. Use `ForEach` when the source is a signal or when you explicitly want a component boundary.
3. **Keep the same names for the non-native helpers**: `ForEach`, `View.of`, `Signal`, `computed`, `State`. These are the cross-language anchors.
4. **Keep `(item, index)` order** for `ForEach` to match JS `map` and Java `BiFunction`. Kotlin/Rust authors can name the lambda params; the order stays documented.
5. **Adapt construction, not semantics.** Java’s `make` builder, Kotlin’s trailing-lambda builders, Rust’s structs/`with`, and TS’s props functions are all valid spellings of the same three operations (`values`, `modifiers`, `children`).
6. **Same wire contract.** The surface differences never change emitted bytes; `ForEach`/`View.of` are still component slots with delta-only emission.

## Two current gaps to acknowledge

- The TypeScript plan on `feat/ts-dsl` is currently **static** (“no structural re-evaluation in phase 1”). It should adopt the same reactive body + `ForEach`/`View.of` semantics when structural reactivity lands.
- Rust parity is Phase 2: `build()` is still host-rebuild + diff, and `Conditional` remains until then. The cross-language contract should mark that as a parity gap, not a different semantic.

- [ ] **Persisted state** — `State<T>` keyed fields (or the language's
  equivalent wiring) against a platform-neutral store ([§3.3](#33-persisted-state-statet)).
- [ ] **Gestures** — `.onTapGesture` (composed from raw pointer down/up) and
  raw `pointerEvents`/`EVENT_LISTENERS` bitmask ([§4.4](#44-gestures)).

   declare intent.

   emitter diffs. A generated DSL must keep the retained tree + emitter

| supply children | `.children(…)` | `.Children(…)` | `.children(vec![…])` / `vstack![…]` | ctor args / `.Children(…)` | `.children(*v)` |
| creation + chaining | static on the view; chain on the returned builder | static on the view; chain via **extension methods** | associated fn `Type::new`; chain via a **trait** + macros | package ctor; chain via methods | kwargs + methods |

 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment |

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005

 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Java DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/`pathland-render-gtk` + tests
 4. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.

 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

   materialized copy gets a distinct node id. The emitter enforces the frame's
   **unique-node-id invariant** (spec/OPCODE.md §Frame Lifecycle) with
   `Emitter.duplicateIds` / a fail-loud guard at mount, resync, and after each
   structural reconcile, so an id-overriding pass (an identity-stable node pinning
   a playback key) can never silently corrupt an id-keyed consumer.

   explicit-router and **router-agnostic** overloads). **Any component can change
   the route** (spec DSL.md §4.5): `Button.make(b -> …).modifiers(NavigationIntent.navigate/push/replace(path))`

   `NavOp` intent on the node; the emitter resolves it to the **nearest
   enclosing** `Router` (the `NavigationContainer` the component lives under)
   during the retained-tree walk and exposes it on

   `tapActions`), which the host routes on tap before `tapActions`. The route is a
   **plain signal** (not persisted; the URL is the web's persistence layer) and
   the host **seeds it before mount** via `navigate(...)` — no `Location`, no
   environment-carried route. A `NAVIGATE` event (`Event.navigate(url)` /
   `Event.navigateBack()`, wire round-trip via `FrameCodec`) routes into the
   router through `RenderResult.navigateHandler`.

   both directions, `encodeEvents`/`decodeEvents` (host→guest events with
   `TEXT_CHANGED` string-section offsets), and **`META::ENVIRONMENT`**

   environment: viewport + initial route; SSR synthesizes it from the request,
   the DOM client sends/enriches it over the WebSocket).

   `PathlandCore.ringMut(handle)` borrows the underlying ring for the in-process
   GTK renderer (`pathland_gtk_run_ring`), and `RingOpcodeSink` is the zero-copy
   guest writer.

   `RenderResult` registries (tap / navigate / text / value / date, `NAVIGATE`
   URL → active path, back → router). Shared by the server session
   (`PathlandSession.dispatch`) and the native GTK host, so both route events
   identically and neither reaches into view internals.

   `BINDING_ID` (= the node's id) on every text/value/date-bound control so the
   GTK renderer's transport-aware event guard fires (`TEXT_CHANGED` /
   `VALUE_CHANGED`). The frame (SSR) path never emits it, keeping server output
   unchanged.

   `pathland-view-processor`.

   emitter sends token refs as the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (path in the frame's
   string section / arena) in both `FrameOpcodeSink` and `RingOpcodeSink`

   builders (`color`/`f32`/`u32`/`u8`/`string`) for one scheme; `AdaptiveTheme(light,

   (`emit`/`emitInto`); `Theme.emit`/`AdaptiveTheme.emit` write one frame of
   `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides (the dark theme's with the `dark.` prefix),
   and `OpcodeSink.setDesignToken` puts path + STRING values into the string
   section (frame) / arena (ring). The `Emitter` takes a `ThemeData` and rides it
   into the mount + resync frames. Overrides are renderer-global — they never
   re-emit nodes.
 - **Non-color token refs**: `Length` (`Length.of(float)` / `Length.token(path)`)
   is accepted by `Padding`, `FontSize`, stack/grid `spacing`, `Border` width,
   `CornerRadius`, and `Frame` width/height; `FontFamily.Token` covers the
   `FONT_FAMILY` STRING token. The emitter detects `TokenPath` and sends
   `DESIGN_TOKEN`; literal/signal values keep their existing forms.
 - **Runtime theming**: `Emitter.replaceTheme(ThemeData)` / `resetTheme()` and
   `setColorScheme(ThemeMode)`; `PathlandSession.setTheme` / `resetTheme` /
   `setColorScheme` delegate to the same emission path. Replacement emits
   `META::RESET_THEME` + overrides in one frame; `ThemeMode` is
   `PLATFORM`/`LIGHT`/`DARK`. `OpcodeSink.resetTheme`/`setColorScheme` are
   implemented by both the frame and ring sinks.
 
 ## Not implemented / gaps
 
 - `ACTION_ID`/`BINDING_ID` are usable as modifiers (`actionId`/`bindingId`); the
   Java model routes events by node id through the emitter's registries
   (`RenderResult`), so the frame (SSR) path does not set them automatically.
   On the ring (desktop) path the emitter auto-sets `BINDING_ID` for bound
   controls (see Implemented) — the GTK renderer gates value/text events on it.
 - Structural reconcile does not emit `SET_PROPERTY` for a *removed* property on
   a matched node (the wire has no unset; the renderer keeps the last value) —
   consistent with the Rust engine.

 `mvn test` (JDK 17+) — emitter, codec round-trips (incl. `NAVIGATE`), signals,
-state, reactive bodies (`ReactiveBodyTest`), reactive slots (`ViewOfTest`) and the
-router (`RouterTest`:
+state, reactive bodies (`ReactiveBodyTest`), reactive slots (`ViewOfTest`),
+reactive lists (`ForEachTest`) and the router (`RouterTest`:

 fallback, `NAVIGATE` routing, `NavigationLink`, the **declarative nav
 intents** (`.navigate/.push/.replace` + router-agnostic `NavigationLink`

 **`Navigation` facade / `Params` / `isActive`**, the **scoped environment
 values** (`View.environment` + `Environment.value` hierarchy/restore), and the

   `RangeConfig`, …) with fluent setters, consumed by the value builders. Values
